section_summary: This section opens with 1941 press clippings about proposed investigations of Japanese consular activity, overseas conscription, propaganda allegations, and the credibility of Korean publicist Kilsoo Haan. A 1942 embassy despatch then reproduces detailed Japanese draft-deferment instructions and application forms issued in Argentina. Later telegrams, correspondence, and memoranda concern Japan’s extension of compulsory service, recruitment in occupied Beijing, the military obligations of American-born Japanese who renounced Japanese nationality, and the overseas distribution of Japanese Army divisions.

subfiles.title: Press clippings on Japanese consular activity, propaganda, and overseas conscription
subfiles.from: National Citizens League; Honolulu Star-Bulletin; The New York Times; Hawaii Hochi; The Rafu Shimpo
subfiles.about: A compilation of 1941 reports and commentary on proposed investigations of Japanese organizations, consular activities, propaganda allegations, and conscription measures affecting Japanese residents in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Clippings: the National Citizens League denies Japanese affiliations and demands investigation of Gillette and Haan allegations; editorials question Haan's credibility; Gillette consults Hull; Knox warns of rapid conflict.

subfiles.title: Japanese Military Draft Deferment Applications in Argentina
subfiles.from: Edward L. Reed, Counselor of Embassy, Buenos Aires, for the Ambassador
subfiles.about: Reports and translates Japanese Consulate procedures for draft deferment, declarations of overseas residence, and military-age registration in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: Reed reports that the Japanese Consulate in Buenos Aires had advertised daily instructions for the 1943 draft year and concludes that Japanese men aged nineteen through thirty-seven were then subject to conscription. The enclosed notice, dated November 18, 1942, requires applications between December 1 and January 31 and specifies which birth cohorts need new approval or reapproval of deferment. Forms A through C collect Japanese registry and Argentine residence information, occupational and educational details, and abilities such as riding, swimming, jujitsu, and fencing.

subfiles.title: Telegram on extension of Japanese obligatory military service
subfiles.about: Transmits German military commentary on Japan's extension of compulsory service to men aged nineteen to twenty and forty to forty-four.
subfiles.summary: Commentator: newly covered age groups would not be called immediately but could be mobilized quickly; men 40-44 would do auxiliary defense duty.

subfiles.title: Airgram reporting recruitment of Japanese civilians in Peiping
subfiles.about: Reports that Japanese civilian males aged eighteen to thirty in the Beijing area were being ordered into the armed forces and sent to Japan for training.
subfiles.summary: Drumright relays a Chinese student's account that Japanese civilian men aged 18-30 in Beijing were ordered into the armed forces and to Japan for training.

subfiles.title: Inquiry concerning American-born Japanese and military service in Japan
subfiles.from: Charles E. Burbridge, Cowichan Station, British Columbia
subfiles.about: Asks whether Japanese law required fit American-born Japanese men who had renounced Japanese nationality to perform military service in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Burbridge asks whether US-born men of Japanese parents remained liable for Japanese military service after lawful renunciation.

subfiles.title: Reply directing Burbridge to the State Department
subfiles.from: Lloyd W. Schram, Bureau of Governmental Research, University of Washington
subfiles.about: Advises Burbridge to ask the State Department about the military status in Japan of American-born Japanese.
subfiles.summary: Schram refers Burbridge's question on military duty of American-born Japanese to the State Department in Washington.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Vancouver regarding Burbridge's nationality inquiry
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in Charge, Vancouver
subfiles.about: Provides a proposed answer to Burbridge's question about renunciation of Japanese nationality and military service.
subfiles.summary: Instruction: Japan's 1899 nationality law as amended in 1924 did not legally prevent renunciation before service, but military authorities commonly required such persons to serve.

subfiles.title: Distribution of Japanese Army divisions
subfiles.about: Lists the geographic distribution of forty-three Japanese Army divisions and associated brigades.
subfiles.summary: Memo places eight divisions in Manchuria and twenty-three elsewhere in China, with others in Indochina, Japan, Korea, Sakhalin and Taiwan.
